content: The Global Dementia Observatory (GDO) Reference Guide, developed by the World Health Organization (WHO), provides a comprehensive framework for addressing dementia as a public health priority. It allows for the adaptation, redistribution, and use of its content for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. The guide emphasizes that the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under equivalent Creative Commons terms. Translations of the guide must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the accuracy of the translation, and the original English version remains the authoritative edition. Dementia is described as a progressive condition that affects memory, cognitive abilities, and behavior, significantly impairing daily living activities. Alzheimer’s disease is the most common form, accounting for 60–70% of cases, followed by vascular dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies, and frontotemporal dementia. Mixed forms of dementia are also common. Globally, approximately 50 million people are affected by dementia, with this number expected to rise to 82 million by 2030 and 152 million by 2050. Nearly 60% of individuals with dementia live in lowand middle-income countries, where most new cases are anticipated. Dementia is the seventh leading cause of death worldwide and a major contributor to disability and dependency among older adults, impacting not only individuals but also their caregivers, families, and communities. In 2012, WHO launched the report Dementia: A Public Health Priority in collaboration with Alzheimer’s Disease International to raise awareness and advocate for action at national and international levels. This was followed by the First Ministerial Conference on Global Action Against Dementia in 2015, which emphasized the importance of monitoring global and national efforts to address dementia. The Global Dementia Observatory (GDO) was established to collect and disseminate data on key dementia indicators, supporting countries in responding to the needs of individuals with dementia and their caregivers. The GDO framework includes three domains—policy, service delivery, and information/research—aligned with seven strategic themes that correspond to the global action plan on dementia for 2017–2025. The GDO framework aims to strengthen health and social care systems by assessing the availability and implementation of dementia-related policies, legislation, and guidelines. It also evaluates resources for sustainable care, from prevention to end-of-life care, and provides comparative epidemiological data to estimate disease prevalence, mortality, and financial impact. The framework supports evidence-based service planning, capacity building, and the development of national research agendas. The guide outlines the process for data collection, recommending the identification of a focal point within each country to coordinate efforts. An online data collection tool, the GDO e-tool, is available in multiple languages to streamline the process. The tool includes specific questions and sub-questions to guide users in providing relevant data, with automatic skipping of non-applicable sections. Data is finalized and submitted to WHO only after confirmation by the focal point. The guide also provides detailed instructions for countries to identify and access relevant data sources, such as national health information systems, ministries of health and social affairs, and professional institutions. It emphasizes the importance of using comprehensive data sources and documenting any deviations from recommended sources. WHO collaborates with international partners to reduce the burden of data collection by linking to existing databases, such as the Global Health Observatory and the OECD. The GDO indicators are closely aligned with the global action plan on dementia, with specific indicators used to monitor progress toward global targets. These indicators are highlighted in the guide for easy reference. The guide also addresses common questions, such as how to handle partial responses or discrepancies in definitions, and provides guidance for reconciling differences. The guide emphasizes the need for a broad public health approach to dementia, involving government and multiple stakeholders to develop comprehensive responses. The inclusion of people with dementia and their caregivers in policy development is crucial for success. The guide provides detailed definitions and methods for estimating key indicators, such as the existence of dementia-specific policies, plans, and funding, as well as targets for monitoring implementation. It also highlights the importance of integrating dementia into related national plans, such as those for mental health, aging, or non-communicable diseases. In summary, the GDO Reference Guide serves as a vital tool for countries to address the complex needs of individuals with dementia and their caregivers, supporting the development of effective policies, services, and research initiatives.
